rewrites.summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors: official WorldPride 2026 guidance confirms visas and entry depend only on nationality, not gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed at the border. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and since July 2025 a discriminatory motive is a statutory aggravating factor that can increase penalties by up to a third.

Practical safety supports are strong: Amsterdam operates dedicated reporting networks for LGBTQIA+ incidents, the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents for 2026, and the capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime. Same-sex marriage is legal and non-binary people are recognised, so a trans traveller's partner status raises no border or legal problems.

The genuine caution is rising reported hostility: discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people reached 4,800 last year, up 51% in a year for transgender-specific reports and 81% since 2022, and many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this chiefly means a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National policy turbulence is pending rather than in force: a self-identification gender-recognition bill was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; neither currently changes the border or discrimination rules a visitor faces.

Comparative context: the nation ranks #13 on a comparative rights map and #2 of 121 regions as a "good place", with public support at 52%; at the same time there is no statutory definition of "hate crime" at national level, the police recording hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a dedicated expertise centre.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The legal gender-recognition (LGR) process still requires an expert letter, falling short of self-determination: the self-identification bill (Transgender Act) was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months — all resident-facing.

Resident-facing victimisation data: official figures record that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people report physical or sexual violence (17% of trans respondents, 22% of intersex people), a third of police discrimination reports in 2022 concerned sexual orientation, only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were recorded last year, and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Pickpocketing, bike theft and taxi scams are general tourist risks affecting everyone, including in the capital, Amsterdam.

Unresolved: the reporting platform describes its Pride-period figure (70+ reports) as "only a fraction of the total", so true incident volume is unverified; the documented enforcement gap (six convictions against 4,800 reports) is real but its practical effect on visitors is unquantified.

rewrites.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk a trans visitor faces: since January 2025 an executive order makes all identity documents issued by the national government reflect sex assigned at birth, the "X" marker was eliminated (the passport agency stopped processing it and markers not matching birth sex, and new applications list only M or F per supporting documents), and mismatched documents have left trans travellers stranded abroad. Airport screening can be invasive and risks outing trans travellers through secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs. A trans traveller was detained at the border for weeks and then deported (January 2025), and a border officer faces a lawsuit over alleged sexual contact with a trans traveller at a major airport.

Enforcement reaches daily life: in April 2025 a trans woman was arrested and jailed overnight under a state's bathroom-restriction law — believed to be the first such arrest — and in another state a trans man was detained for using a women's restroom. Bathroom laws and misgendering statutes vary by state; some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances, while other parts of the country and major cities retain strong protections. Four states are now flagged "do not travel" for trans people, the latest in July 2026.

There is no national sodomy law and no nationwide bathroom ban, so safety is genuinely state-by-state: a trans visitor should check recent violence reports for the destination before travelling, and should expect the passport mismatch risk to dominate the border experience even in otherwise welcoming cities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Parent-nation policy turbulence and litigation flux: the January 2025 executive orders are being challenged in federal courts — a civil-liberties organisation sued the passport agency over document policy, and the national court recently allowed the agency to change trans passport treatment — while a 2026 state law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences not matching birth sex is promoted as a template for other states, with more targeting bills pending in state legislatures.

Neighbour comparison: after the 2025 rollbacks, at least eight allied governments (including two named European ones) adjusted their travel guidance for trans and non-binary citizens entering the country, and the advisories followed documented detentions of foreign citizens over visa issues.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Birth-register and identity practice: one state's 2026 law invalidates birth certificates and driver's licences that do not reflect sex assigned at birth and bars trans people from sex-segregated facilities, and marker-change rules for licences, birth certificates and name changes vary widely state-to-state; rights groups call the law a template that other state legislatures can copy.

The 2026 legislative season continued degrading trans rights across many state legislatures while national policies drove nationwide trends — resident-facing legislative weather rather than border-facing rules.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Gun violence, mass-shooter risk, petty theft and traffic safety are general travel risks affecting everyone.

Unresolved or unverifiable: the lawsuit against the border officer is ongoing, so the alleged conduct is unproven; no official count exists of trans travellers detained, stripped of documents or stranded; state-by-state "do not travel" flags rest on dated risk assessments; and the document rules above can change quickly by executive action, so the passport posture should be re-checked immediately before travel.

rewrites.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Official assessments from a foreign body conclude that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. Enforcement focuses on public expression and activism rather than private existence, and same-sex activity itself is not criminalised — a discreet visitor is not automatically targeted — but there is effectively no police protection, and detention carries placement by passport sex.

One region, Chechnya, where quasi-Sharia governance applies, is in a separate and graver category of danger for anyone perceived as LGBT.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Enforcement flux: extremism-designation prosecutions are the moving part of the regime — convictions passed one hundred by June 2025 and propaganda-law cases have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, so the enforcement surface a visitor could touch keeps expanding rather than stabilising.

The designation has fuelled a purge and mass emigration of LGBT residents and pushed people into silence, flight and self-censorship — signals of a national crackdown trend rather than a stable legal equilibrium; fines from propaganda statutes alone exceeded 60 million rubles into the national budget in two years.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2023 legal-gender-recognition and gender-affirming-care bans are resident-facing; the extremism-designation machinery (convictions, NGO liquidation) targets resident organisations and individuals.

Resident-facing documentation: coercive conversion practice is recorded — a trans woman was held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre before escaping when police responded to a phone she found — and the post-designation climate has driven mass emigration with many trans residents describing emigration as the only means of survival.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Official travel advisories from a foreign government (the US State Department) and most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, due to the risk of wrongful detention, the war in Ukraine, and arbitrary law enforcement.

Unresolved or unverifiable: the travel-advisory page itself could not be retrieved at research time (the underlying highest-level advisory includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers); the death-in-custody case has no published outcome; exact current conviction totals and detention counts are not published, so visitor exposure is assessed from dated records.

Independent reporting (June 2024): after the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, for many transgender residents emigration has become the only means of survival; profiles those caught in limbo between leaving and staying.

Reporting (Jan 2024): within 48 hours of the designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars — about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed — with at least two other venues raided the same night.

rewrites.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban — the nation's current ruling movement — is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 Morality Law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The applicable legal regime is layered and shifting: penal-code "sodomy" provisions carry up to two years, while a Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity and the 2024 Morality Law added surveillance duties; flogging documented by international experts nearly doubled in 2025 to at least 1,110 people.

Asylum-framework context: international guidance treats LGBTIQ people in the country as those perceived to transgress religious and social norms, and refugee-led organisations abroad document systematic persecution — context for the regime's treatment, not visitor-facing advice.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing documentation: trans and gay residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the 2021 takeover; security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in earlier rule.

Interview-based reports from residents in-country and abroad record physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations, with visibly transgender people facing the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor to Afghanistan, independent of any personal characteristic.

Unresolved or unverifiable: enforcement figures rest on 2022-23 interview-based reports and 2025-26 international flogging counts rather than the regime's own statistics; most accounts predate the 2024 Morality Law's implementation, so current on-the-ground practice is inferred rather than directly documented; no tourist entry pathway exists to test in practice.

rewrites.summary:
The United Kingdom has a documented, in-force rollback concentrated on facilities and detention that directly affects trans visitors. Bathroom and changing-room use is now directed by biological sex under the equality watchdog's statutory code — a daily, nationwide civil restriction (the only country above 0.55 in this dataset with a nationally-legislated bathroom restriction). Since the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling, two severe-when-triggered risks apply if arrested: police forces strip-search trans women according to biological sex (with male officers), and trans women are placed in men's prisons — with documented suicide-risk litigation.

Documented trans killings have occurred (2023 and others). The climate is actively deteriorating via court- and equality-watchdog-led rollback rather than executive demonisation — a contrast with the United States.

The traveller-relevant positives are limited: no trans-specific border friction (foreign passports with X or amended markers are accepted), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (in practice theoretical recourse), no criminalisation, and functional institutions. Regional police forces, including the transport police, have published biological-sex search policies. Visitors arrested face the same strip-search and prison-placement rules as residents.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation and policy flux: the prison-placement rules are actively contested — a mid-2026 judgment held that sex-segregated placement must rest on a lawful basis, while human-rights arguments that birth-sex placement of trans prisoners would breach rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk are before the same court; the equality watchdog's single-sex-spaces code came into force in 2026; and revisions to the equality statute drew warnings from international experts (the UN). One devolved region's assessment of the ruling's impact is still pending.

Neighbour comparison: the rollback is court-led, in contrast to executive-led rollback in the United States.

rewrites.summary:
Germany is very safe for transgender visitors, with two real caveats. First, far-right street hostility is the most documented concern: roughly 110 of 245 Pride events in 2025 were disrupted or attacked, over half linked to organised far-right networks, so a visitor at Pride or visibly trans in the eastern regions faces elevated harassment. Second, arrest exposure: if arrested, prison placement generally follows your self-chosen civil-registry gender entry under recent state-level reforms, but exceptions allow placement contrary to your self-declared gender and are invoked inconsistently — a provocateur who had self-identified as female was moved from a women's to a men's prison in 2026 after public outcry.

Offsetting factors: bathrooms are unrestricted (venue-level sauna debates only), no border-police humiliation of trans travellers is documented, and carrying personal hormone therapy through the border area is uneventful; the self-identification act is a positive climate signal though not itself a traveller-outing factor.

Calibration note: the nation recorded an ~35% rise in "gender diversity" hate-crime assaults in 2024 (1,152 cases), and a trans DJ filed a legal complaint over degrading security screening at a major airport — a real airport-outing incident, though it went through a functioning legal complaint mechanism.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Neighbour and comparator signals: the constitutional court blocked an extradition to a neighbouring nation on trans-rights grounds, the national government issued trans-traveller warnings about a distant allied nation, and prison placement here is contrasted favourably with a neighbouring nation that places by legal gender and has subjected trans women to invasive "verification" checks.

National policy turbulence (2025-26): a governing-coalition proposal to designate some countries 'safe countries of origin' despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there; an education minister's ban on gender-inclusive language in a ministry, which the national anti-discrimination office said contradicts constitutional equality protection; and the announced end of humanitarian admission programmes including one for persecuted LGBTI refugees.

Litigation and reform flux on prison placement: several state-level prison statutes were amended and a new state prison act took effect in early 2026 with no press coverage; a criminological research institute records that the penal system runs on binary men/women housing with identity-conforming placement only exceptional.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-identification act's civil-registry procedure and the state-level prison-placement reforms are resident-facing administrative law; the prison-placement exceptions and their inconsistent invocation affect resident detainees.

Resident-facing documentation: a criminological research institute records that placement conforming to gender identity is practised only in exceptional cases; sauna-venue guidelines restricting women's saunas to persons whose 'primary sex characteristics correspond' set off a public debate about registered trans women's access; official prison-services pages for trans, inter and non-binary people in custody exist across facilities.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General urban crime is low; standard travel precautions suffice. The far-right street activity flagged affects Pride events and some eastern regions disproportionately.

Unresolved or unverifiable: the airport-screening complaint's outcome is not reported beyond the filing; the provocateur's reassignment cited the safety of other prisoners, and whether it sets a precedent for ordinary trans visitors is unlitigated; one state's new prison statute took effect with no press coverage, so its practical application is unverified; sauna access remains a venue-by-venue matter with no settled national stance.

rewrites.summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

Same-sex marriage remains unavailable, which matters for a trans visitor planning to travel with a partner on spousal status. One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux: the court-based gender-change route is the moving part of the legal framework — a 2023 ruling struck down the sterilisation requirement and another ruled workplace bathroom restrictions illegal the same year, while full marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent; the 2023 "understanding" law was enacted only after months of debate and watering-down amid a culture-war contest.

A dated 2009 shadow report documents invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation plus discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention at the time — a baseline for comparing how far institutional protection has moved.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The court-based legal gender change process, the 2023 sterilisation ruling, and the workplace-bathroom ruling are resident-facing; the onsen challenge is traveller-facing and stays in the summary.

Resident-facing documentation: the 2023 rulings favouring transgender employees arose from long-running workplace disputes; one ruling held that barring a trans woman from the women's bathroom at work violated public-service law, with a lower court awarding damages in 2019 on her 'important legal interest' to live by her self-identified gender.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Natural disasters (earthquakes, typhoons) are the principal travel risk and affect everyone.

Unresolved or unverifiable: no trans-specific travel advisory exists; the culture-war current is assessed from legislative-debate reporting rather than street-level data; marriage-equality status can shift, so spousal-travel assumptions should be re-checked before travel; the 2009 baseline predates the 2023 rulings and is retained only for trend context.

rewrites.summary:
Ireland is a calm, comfortable destination for transgender visitors. It was one of the first countries to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration — the 2015 Gender Recognition Act lets adults change their legal gender without medical requirements — and bathroom use is unrestricted. A hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity took effect at the end of 2024, equality law bans discrimination in employment, housing and services, and marriage equality was approved by referendum in 2015.

The caveats are stagnation and a mildly worsening climate rather than active rollback. The 2015 law is binary-only and long-promised reform (non-binary, under-16s) has stalled; transphobic hate speech remains uncriminalised after a 2024 government U-turn; a university study in 2025 documented rising discrimination against sexual and gender minorities; and total hate-crime reports rose about 15% in 2025 (racism and xenophobia are the most common motives). None of this amounts to criminal exposure or physical danger for a visitor.

Day-to-day, the country is welcoming with low violent crime and a strong civil-society support network.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Policy flux: the stalled non-binary and under-16 reform and the 2024 government U-turn on criminalising transphobic hate speech are national legislative standings that shape the climate; comparative positioning is strong — one of only a handful of countries allowing gender recognition through self-determination with no psychological evaluation, and ranked among the highest regions for public support.

The decade since self-declaration has seen renewed calls over remaining gaps, and hate-crime reporting under the 2024 act is young, so trend lines are still forming.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2015 Gender Recognition Act (binary-only, stalled non-binary/under-16 reform) is a resident-facing process.

Resident-facing barriers: years-long waiting lists for multidisciplinary gender-care assessment are pushing some trans people towards unofficial channels, documented in 2025; a university study found discrimination against sexual and gender minorities has increased despite the protective framework.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory exists; general urban crime is low.

Unresolved or unverifiable: the official police hate-crime statistics page returned no usable finding at research time (the 15% rise rests on news reporting); a 2024 news report on the hate-speech U-turn could not be retrieved, though the still-uncriminalised status is documented elsewhere; conversion therapy remains not banned and intersex surgery is unaddressed — statuses that may change.
